See also: nøgen

Danish

Etymology

From Old Danish nokær, nogher, noghen, from Old Norse nǫkkurr, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk nokon and Swedish någon. Grammaticalization of the phrase Proto-Germanic *ne wait ek hwarjaz (“I don't know who = somebody”). For the expression, compare Old English nāthwylc (“somebody”) (from *ne wāt hwylċ), Middle High German neizwer (“somebody”) (from *ne weiz wer), Latin nescio quis (“somebody”).

The Danish form has -n from the old accusative, cf. Old Norse nǫkkurn, whereas the plural the old -r- has been replaced by -l- in the plural nogle, cf. Old Norse nǫkkura, Swedish några. The neuter noget contains a different pronoun than the rest of the paradigm: Old Norse nǫkkut, Norwegian Nynorsk noko, Swedish något, from Proto-Germanic *ne wait ek hwat.

Pronunciation

  • IPA(key): /noːɣən/, [ˈnoːn̩], [ˈnoːn], [ˈnoŋŋ̩]
  • Homophone: nogle

Pronoun

nogen (neuter noget, plural nogle or nogen)

  1. (determiner) some
  2. (pronoun) somebody, someone, something

Usage notes

  • In spoken language, the plural most often has the form nogen.

Pronoun

nogen (neuter noget, plural nogen)

  1. (determiner) any
  2. (pronoun) anybody, anyone, anything

Usage notes

  • This pronoun is used in questions and negative sentences.

Norwegian Bokmål

Etymology 1

Norwegian Wikipedia has an article on:
Karaktersystemer i Norge
Wikipedia no

Clipping of nogenlunde (“bare pass (school grade)”), an older spelling of noenlunde.

The components of the source word go back to Old Norse nǫkkurr (“some, any”) (from Proto-Norse) and Old Norse lund (“manner, disposition”), with earlier ancestry in Proto-Germanic and Proto-Indo-European; see noenlunde for the full component histories.

Pronunciation

  • IPA(key): /²ˈnoː.ɡən/, [ˈnôː.ɡən], [ˈnôː.ɡn̩]
  • Rhymes: -oːɡən
  • Hyphenation: no‧gen

Noun

nogen m (definite singular nogenen, indefinite plural nogener, definite plural nogenene)

  1. (education, colloquial, historical) a bare pass; a low school grade called nogenlunde tilfredsstillende or nokså godt in older Norwegian grading systems
    Han fikk en nogen i regning. ― He received a bare pass in arithmetic.
    • 1997 July 26, Dagens Næringsliv, page 26:
      karakterboken viste to megeter, tre nogener og resten g’er
      the report card showed two grades of “very good”, three bare passes and “good” for the rest
    • 2000 July 19, Aftenposten, Oslopuls, page 19:
      […] Som belønnet innsatsen med karakteren Nogen
      […] Who rewarded the effort with a bare pass
Derived terms
  • Ng (“bare pass (school grade)”) (abbreviation)

Etymology 2

Alternative forms

  • noen (current standard spelling)

Pronunciation

  • IPA(key): /²ˈnuː.ən/, [ˈnûː.ən], [ˈnûː.n̩]
  • Rhymes: -uːən
  • Homophone: noen
  • Hyphenation: no‧gen

Pronoun

nogen (neuter noget, plural nogen or nogle)

  1. superseded spelling of noen (“some, any; someone, anyone”)
    Har du nogen penger? ― Do you have any money?
    Det er nogen ved døren. ― There is someone at the door.
    • 1873, Henrik Ibsen, Kejser og Galilæer, page 52:
      nogen har forrådt mig
      someone has betrayed me
    • 1882, Henrik Ibsen, En folkefiende, page 96:
      stryg ikke nogen af udråbstegnene!
      do not cross out any of the exclamation marks!
    • 1908, Knut Hamsun, Rosa, page 28:
      hun sa nogen svenske ord i blandt
      she said a few Swedish words now and then
    • 1911, Sigrid Undset, Jenny, page 304:
      for nogen farver
      what colours
Usage notes

The pronoun spelling nogen was removed from official Bokmål orthography in 1938; noen had been permitted as a secondary form since 1917.[1] This does not apply to the school-grade noun above.

Older written usage distinguished plural nogle (“some”) from nogen (“any”), while colloquial Norwegian used nogen for both.[2]
